title: Miserable life, tragic death ; Coroner's inquest examines how Martin Blackwind's life ended on a bloodsoaked prison mattress
article: Paramedic Edward Dunk remembers well the early-morning dispatch call that sent his ambulance to the Warkworth Penitentiary \-- "going with lights and sirens" -- as being a "possible VSA", as in "vital signs absent."

Prison guard Keith Payne, however, remembers it differently -- in that inmate Martin Blackwind, suspected of having no more than slashed his wrist, was still breathing on his own right up until the ambulance arrived, and that his blood-soaked mattress had gone unnoticed until the bed was tossed back to give the ambulance attendants more room.

By then, however, Martin Blackwind was as good as dead, and his ride in the back of the ambulance -- in handcuffs and leg irons, supposedly as per protocol -- a mere formality on the way to his death being officially pronounced by the emergency room doctor at Campbellford Memorial Hospital.

After 18 months in limbo, put on hold until the OPP investigated possible criminal charges against corrections officers at the prison, the coroner's inquest into Martin Blackwind's in\-custody death in October 2006, finally began here yesterday, presided over by regional coroner Dr. Peter Clark.
Booked to run eight more days, it will not be a short-haul inquest, not with early testimony and time frames already at odds.

According to the security computer in the control room at Warkworth, for example, Martin Blackwind, having sliced open the main artery in his upper arm, and now dealing with a change of heart over his attempt at suicide, had pushed the emergency button in his cell at precisely 2:37:55 a.m. on the last day of his miserable life.
And it was a miserable life.

If anyone personified the stereotypical image of the "drunken Indian," this 52-year-old native originally from the Sioux Village Reserve in Manitoba was that image and more -- a homeless, Listerine-swilling alcoholic since childhood who slept on a hot-air vent in downtown Toronto and who, for the second time in his life, had killed a woman who shared his lifestyle, his addiction and his squalor.

Even Martin Blackwind himself would agree, judging by all the wrist slashings and deep scars from previous suicide attempts that autopsy pictures vividly put on display -- all which begs one question yet to be answered by this inquest.
Why did Martin Blackwind have in his possession a nifty prison craft kit that came complete with not only miniature screwdrivers, but a scalpel-like knife with spare blades?
And why did ambulance attendant Edward Dunk not get his dispatch call until 2:56 a.m., a full 18 minutes after the alarm first sounded in the prison's control room?
Why the delay?
According to Payne, corrections directives were to blame, with rules insisting three guards be present before any inmate's cell is opened, regardless of the circumstances.

And Payne, as he testified, was alone in that range and that part of the prison when Blackwind sounded the alarm, and that it took time to assess the situation, get the proper authorization to summon an ambulance because no nurse was on duty during the night shift, and then more time to hussle up the required backup to enter Blackwind's cell.

Add another 13 minutes for the ambulance's run to the prison, five minutes more to get clearance through the prison gates, and another few minutes to get to Cell 17-A, and Martin Blackwind was not only drained of time but drained of blood.

When Blackwind wound up dying in custody -- his history both sordid and murderous -- Corrections Canada issued a news release that seemed almost clinical in its portrayal of a textbook response -- how Blackwind was discovered with "potentially life-threatening injuries" and how an ambulance was called "immediately."

Then came a scathing report in Blackwind's death -- documented here as part of a 15-part series on the urban aboriginal -- in which federal prison investigator Howard Sapers lambasted the correctional system for falling short of its mandate for preserving life, as well as systematic discrimination when it came to First Nations inmates.
Inquests, by law, cannot apply blame, and can only make recommendations to how similar deaths can be prevented.

While it is early into the game, short-staffing is already coming onto the radar screen at the inquest here into Blackwind's death and how, on weekends and at night, the penitentiary at Warkworth, home to upwards of 600 inmates, has no nursing staff on duty to make medical assessments, and no staff psychologist to deal with suicidal behaviours.
Tuesday, prison guard Keith Payne will continue to have his testimony cross-examined by Sheila Cuthbertson, a lawyer with Aboriginal Legal Services of Toronto.

Her last question Monday had Payne admitting that Martin Blackwind was cuffed and shackled for his final ride to hospital -- even though paramedic Edward Dunk arrived to find the inmate lying on the floor, without a pulse and not breathing.
In other words, he was VSA.
Blackwind's official cause of death, said forensic pathologist Dr. Nihad Ali-Ridha, was exsanguination.
His blood, as it turned out, was in his mattress.
